newsitem.title: CHINA: China satellite launch boosts troubled sector.
newsitem.headline: China satellite launch boosts troubled sector.

text.p: China successfully fired a domestic telecommunications satellite into orbit on Monday in a launch seen boosting its space industry and possibly cutting insurance costs after a string of high-profile failures.

A Long March 3A rocket fired the Dongfanghong-3 (East is Red) communications satellite into orbit just after midnight from the Xichang launch centre in southwestern Sichuan province, a spokeswoman for China Aerospace Corp said by telephone.
"The rocket launch was entirely successful," the spokeswoman said. "(We) are currently continuing to track the satellite."

International satellite insurers had been waiting for the launch of the Dongfanghong-3 after the failure of two major launches last year, saying a third loss could further drive up inflated premiums on Chinese launches.
"This is a major step forward for China Great Wall," said John Salaverry, president of space insurance brokers ISB Asia/Pacific, based in Singapore.
"After taking a long time to make sure that everything was right, they've finally done it," he said.
The launch was preceded late last year by a modest victory for China's space industry when it launched and then successfully retrieved according to plan a scientific research satellite.
That came after a $230-million Intelsat 708 satellite was lost in February 1996 when its rocket veered off course and exploded, killing six people on the ground.
Last August, a U.S.-built domestic communications satellite was stranded in a useless orbit by a Long March 3 rocket.

Industry sources said last week that the launch of the Dongfanghong-3 satellite, which was built by China Great Wall Industries Corp, had been rescheduled from May 5 because China's space authorities wanted to be sure that all would go well.
The satellite, owned by a subsidiary of China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, was launched at 12.17 a.m. on Monday (1617 GMT Sunday), the China Aerospace spokeswoman said.
China planned to launch the Fengyun-2, its first domestically made geostationary meteorological satellite, next month, she said.
"In June we will launch the Fengyun-2 and after that we will launch satellites for foreign companies," she said.
China Aerospace officials have said they plan to use their Long March series of rockets to launch more than 30 satellites for other countries in the next four years.
Salaverry said the successful launch would be viewed very positively by the international insurance community.
"But we'll be waiting to see re-confirmation with the second launch," he said.
An official with China Pacific Insurance, one of the insurers for the satellite, said it was difficult to say how the successful launch would affect insurance rates.
A manager with a European insurance group in Shanghai said it would have a positive impact, although not immediately.
"The rates for Chinese satellite launches three or four years ago were around 16 percent, but as a result of the losses they've had, it is now around the 20 percent level," the manager said.
"This launch doesn't do much (to rates) in the first instance, but with two or three more, people will get more confident," he said.
